summary.text: Deep time is the idea of geological time stretching across billions of years, far beyond anything a human life can take in.
Scottish geologist James Hutton developed it in the 18th century, picturing an endless cycle of rocks forming under the sea, being uplifted and tilted, then eroded into new layers.
Charles Lyell's framing of this vast timescale gave Charles Darwin the time his theory of evolution by natural selection needed to seem plausible.

facts.label: Key site
facts.value: Siccar Point unconformity, visited by Hutton in 1788

facts.label: Popularized by
facts.value: Writers such as John McPhee, 20th century

items.prompt: On a sea cliff, you see layers that formed under water, were tilted on end, worn flat, and then buried under fresh flat layers. What would James Hutton have read in this scene?

options.label: One sudden disaster that tore the coast apart
An extremely slow cycle of forming, lifting and eroding rock
Minerals crystallising once out of an ancient global ocean
A few centuries of storms reshaping the shoreline

items.explain: Hutton saw rocks forming under the sea, being uplifted and tilted, then eroded into new layers in an endless cycle, and the cliff at Siccar Point convinced his friends this cycle was extremely slow.

items.prompt: Why did Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection depend on geologists accepting deep time?

options.label: Gradual change in living things seems implausible without a vast span of time
Geologists had already found the first living cell in ancient rock layers
Fossils could only be explained by a series of sudden global disasters
Deep time showed that species never change once they first appear

items.explain: Lyell's deep timescale gave Darwin the time his theory needed; without a vast temporal backdrop, evolutionary change would have seemed implausible.

items.prompt: A 19th-century naturalist argues that Earth's past was broken into chapters, each ended by a disaster and followed by the sudden appearance of new life forms. Which school of thought is this?

options.label: Uniformitarianism
Plutonism
Catastrophism
Neptunism

items.explain: Georges Cuvier's catastrophism saw history as a series of catastrophic events, each followed by new life forms, giving a segmented rather than continuous past.

items.prompt: Charles Lyell argued that slow, everyday processes like erosion, sedimentation and volcanic activity shaped Earth's surface. What did that view imply?

options.label: Earth's surface had barely changed since it formed
Most landscapes were carved in a single great flood
Volcanoes alone were enough to build every continent
Earth was far older than people had previously imagined

items.explain: If gradual processes did the shaping, they needed vast periods to do it, implying an Earth far older than previously imagined.

items.prompt: After a long history of work, scientists settled on an age for the Earth. Roughly how old is it?

options.label: About 4.55 million years
About 455 million years
About 45.5 billion years
About 4.55 billion years

items.explain: The age of the Earth has been determined to be around 4.55 billion years.

items.prompt: Why are nuclear waste repositories used as a real-world case study in planning across deep time?

options.label: They are built from rock that is billions of years old
They must stay secure for tens of thousands of years
They turn waste into fossils within a single human lifetime
They are sited only where the oldest fossils are found

items.explain: Nuclear waste repositories are designed to remain secure for tens of thousands of years, so building them means communicating and planning across deep time scales.
